teaser: Critics laughed and called him a “tubist.” Léger went and painted more tubes.
review_notes:
Check: Louis Vauxcelles's 'tubiste' / 'tubism' jibe dates from 1911 and was aimed at Léger's earlier work (Nudes in the Forest), not at this canvas specifically.
Check: support is burlap (MoMA: oil on burlap, about 100 x 81 cm); series of roughly fifty works in 1913-14.
Check: contract with dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler in 1913.
The image is a photo of the framed painting on a wall; coordinates refer to that photo.

lesson.text: When Fernand Léger first showed his work in Paris, a critic looked at the stovepipe limbs and barrel-shaped bodies and found his joke: this was not Cubism, it was “tubism.” The word stuck. People repeated it with a grin.

Léger could have softened his style. He did the opposite. In 1913 he dropped the bodies, the trees, the rooftops, everything the tubes had been pretending to be, and kept only the tubes. He called the results Contrasts of Forms, and painted about fifty of them.

So there is no hidden figure to hunt for here, though people often try. What you get is a pile of drums, cones and cylinders that seems to tumble down the middle of the canvas between two walls of blue.
Three shapes give you the logic of the whole heap.

lines.label: The big drum
lines.text: A fat rounded form, split by straight lines into wedges of green and white. Curved outline, straight cuts: the first contrast.

lines.label: The fallen cylinder
lines.text: Lower down, a cylinder lies on its side. Its red and green bands are not shading. They are stripes of flat color with white between them.

lines.label: The blue wall
lines.text: Stiff vertical streaks of blue fence the pile in on both sides. Still against tumbling, straight against round.

lesson.text: That is his whole method, and he said so in lectures at the time: a picture gets its force from opposites pushed together. Curve against straight line. Flat patch against rounded volume. Red against green, which are as far apart as two colors can be.
Léger's rule: do not blend, oppose. The more strongly two things differ, the more each one comes alive.
Before he was a painter, Léger worked as an architectural draftsman, drawing plans for a living. The firm black outlines and the love of cylinders and beams never left him.
Now forget the shapes and look at how the thing is made. It is rougher than it seems in a small reproduction, and the roughness is deliberate.

spots.title: White as highlight
spots.text: White is scrubbed onto the middle of each form and the color pushed to its edges. That is enough to make a flat shape bulge like polished metal catching light.

spots.title: Bare cloth
spots.text: In the lower left the paint thins out and the coarse beige fabric shows. Léger chose burlap, a cheap sacking cloth, and let its grain stay visible.

spots.title: A yellow lens
spots.text: One of several almond-shaped yellows scattered across the heap. They work like accents in a rhythm, pulling your eye from top to bottom.

spots.title: The rungs
spots.text: Short black bars stacked like a ladder. A flat, striped motif placed right beside swelling volumes, one more contrast.

spots.title: Unfinished on purpose
spots.text: Red dabs float without filling their outlines. The drawing and the color do not match up, so you sense how fast the picture was built.

lesson.text: Only six ingredients: red, green, blue, yellow, white and a black line. From them Léger gets weight, bulge, clatter and speed without picturing anything. In 1913 very few painters anywhere had gone this far from the visible world.

The series earned him something rare for a young avant-garde painter: a contract. The dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler, who already represented Picasso and Braque, signed him up in 1913, which meant a regular income.

It lasted a year. In August 1914 Léger was called up, and the man who had painted imaginary metal tubes found himself among real ones, the gun barrels of the First World War. What he saw there would send his cylinders in a new direction.

quiz.question: What nickname did a critic give Léger's style?
quiz.explanation: His tube-like forms led to the mocking label “tubism.”

quiz.question: What do the Contrasts of Forms depict?
options: Nothing recognizable: only drums, cones and cylinders
quiz.explanation: Léger dropped all subjects and kept only the forms.

quiz.question: How does Léger make a flat shape look round?
options: With white scrubbed in the middle and color at the edges
quiz.explanation: The white reads as a highlight on a curved surface.

quiz.question: What is the painting made on?
quiz.explanation: The rough beige fabric shows through where the paint is thin.

quiz.question: What was Léger's job before painting?
quiz.explanation: He drew architectural plans, which fed his taste for firm outlines.

facts.text: Léger painted only one picture called Contrast of Forms.
facts.explanation: He painted about fifty works in the series in 1913 and 1914.

facts.text: Léger believed strong opposites give a picture its force.
facts.explanation: He set curve against line, flat against round, red against green.

facts.text: The canvas is evenly covered with smooth paint from edge to edge.
facts.explanation: Bare burlap shows in several places and the color floats loosely inside the outlines.
